date.note: Composed in the sixteenth century in Safed (Tzfat) by Solomon Alkabetz (c. 1500-1576); the year 1540 is an approximate marker for the mid-sixteenth-century Safed setting, not a precise date of composition. The hymn entered the Kabbalat Shabbat ('Welcoming the Sabbath') service that took shape among the Safed kabbalists and thereafter spread across Jewish communities. The digitized Hebrew (Wikisource) and English (Sefaria Community Translation) text on Sefaria carries the opening couplet read for this entry.

summary: Lekha Dodi ('Come, my Beloved') is a liturgical hymn (piyyut) composed in sixteenth-century Safed by Solomon Alkabetz and sung on Friday evening to welcome the Sabbath in the Kabbalat Shabbat service, personifying the Sabbath as a bride whom the community goes out to greet. On Sefaria's rendering it opens 'Come, my lover, to welcome the bride; the face of Shabbat we will receive' (Lekha Dodi 1). Alkabetz's name appears as an acrostic formed by the initial letters of the hymn's stanzas, and its imagery is drawn from the kabbalistic world of Safed: the Sabbath as Queen and Bride, and the exile and hoped-for redemption of Israel and of the Shekhinah (the divine presence). It was adopted into the Friday-night liturgy across Jewish communities.
description:
Lekha Dodi ('Come, my Beloved') is a Sabbath-eve hymn (piyyut) composed in the sixteenth century by Solomon Alkabetz (Shlomo ha-Levi Alkabetz, c. 1500-1576), a kabbalist of Safed (Tzfat) in the Galilee and a brother-in-law of Moses Cordovero. It is sung on Friday evening as the central hymn of Kabbalat Shabbat, the service of 'Welcoming the Sabbath' that took shape among the Safed kabbalists, and the account that follows describes the hymn and its imagery as the tradition's own liturgical creation and attributed meaning rather than as claims the editor affirms.

The hymn's refrain, on the open Sefaria text read for this entry, is 'Come, my lover, to welcome the bride; the face of Shabbat we will receive' (Lekha Dodi 1, Sefaria Community Translation), and it is more commonly rendered in English as 'Come, my Beloved, to meet the bride; the presence of the Sabbath let us welcome'. The refrain personifies the Sabbath as a bride and queen (kallah, malka) whom the worshipping community goes out to greet, a figure the Safed kabbalists connected with the Shekhinah, the indwelling divine presence. The stanzas that follow are built on that image: they call Jerusalem, the 'royal city', to rouse itself from the dust of exile, address Israel in its dispersion, and look toward redemption, closing with the summons to enter 'in peace, O crown of her husband', at which, by the Safed custom the hymn accompanies, the congregation turns to face the entering Sabbath.

Alkabetz signed the hymn by an acrostic: the initial Hebrew letters of the successive stanzas spell out his name, Shlomo ha-Levi (שלמה הלוי). This built-in signature is a recognized feature of the piyyut and the tradition's own testimony to its authorship. The hymn's language draws on the biblical and rabbinic vocabulary of the Sabbath and on the kabbalistic setting of Safed, where the reception of the Sabbath was elaborated into a mystical rite: on the reading current in the scholarship and in the tradition, its bride-and-Queen imagery and its movement from exile to redemption reflect the theosophy of that circle, in which the Sabbath is bound up with the union of the divine presence (the Shekhinah) and the people of Israel, and the exile of Israel is read together with the exile of the Shekhinah. The entry records this mystical construal as the imagery the hymn carries within its tradition, described and attributed, not affirmed as doctrine by the editor.

From its Safed origin the hymn passed into the Friday-night liturgy of communities across the Jewish world, Ashkenazi and Sephardi alike, and it stands today near the close of the Kabbalat Shabbat section of the evening service in the common inheritance of the tradition. This entry presents Lekha Dodi on Judaism's own terms as Alkabetz's sixteenth-century Safed hymn, with its authorship (the acrostic), its kabbalistic imagery (the Sabbath Bride and Queen, the exile and redemption of Israel and the Shekhinah), and its universal liturgical adoption described and attributed, and its mystical meaning recorded as the tradition's rather than adjudicated.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Lekha Dodi ('Come, my Beloved') on Judaism's own terms as the sixteenth-century Sabbath-eve hymn of Solomon Alkabetz of Safed, sung in Kabbalat Shabbat (neutrality #1, #4, #6). Its authorship (the acrostic Shlomo ha-Levi in the initial letters of the stanzas), its Safed-kabbalistic imagery (the Sabbath as Bride and Queen, the exile and redemption of Israel and the Shekhinah), and its adoption across Jewish communities are DESCRIBED and ATTRIBUTED, not affirmed: the hymn's mystical construal is stated as the tradition's own ('on the reading current in the scholarship and in the tradition', 'recorded as the imagery the hymn carries within its tradition', 'not affirmed as doctrine by the editor'), with no devotional register. Sources triangulate three lenses per neutrality #8-#9: (a) academic, Reuven Kimelman, The Mystical Meaning of 'Lekhah Dodi' and 'Kabbalat Shabbat' (Magnes / Cherub Press, 2003), the standard study of the hymn's mystical structure; (b) the PRIMARY text itself, open and auditable on Sefaria (English: Sefaria Community Translation, CC0; Hebrew: Wikisource, CC-BY-SA), the opening refrain (Lekha Dodi 1) READ LINE-BY-LINE; (c) a contemporary Jewish scholar on-topic, Lawrence A. Hoffman (ed.), My People's Prayer Book, Vol. 8: Kabbalat Shabbat (Welcoming Shabbat in the Synagogue) (Jewish Lights, 2005). No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no Jewish Encyclopedia, no My Jewish Learning, no Chabad.org), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE / HONESTY: the Sefaria text of Lekha Dodi is rated HIGH because the opening refrain was READ line-by-line via the open Sefaria text API and confirmed VERBATIM: Lekha Dodi 1 opens 'Come, my lover, to welcome the bride / The face of Shabbat we will receive' (Sefaria Community Translation, CC0; Hebrew לְכָה דוֹדִי לִקְרַאת כַּלָּה, Wikisource CC-BY-SA), the load-bearing text for the hymn's refrain and its personification of the Sabbath as a bride. The full hymn (all ten sections) is open on the same Sefaria text and was read: the AUTHORSHIP acrostic Shlomo ha-Levi (שלמה הלוי) was confirmed from the initial letters of the eight body stanzas read line-by-line, shin (Shamor), lamed (Likrat), mem (Mikdash), he (Hitna'ari), he (Hitoreri), lamed (Lo), vav (Ve-hayu), yod (Yamin), with the concluding stanza (Bo'i, bet) correctly outside the acrostic. The two monographs (Kimelman, Hoffman) are MEDIUM, verified to exist and be on-topic (Magnes/Cherub Press and Jewish Lights records), not read line-by-line; they carry the mystical construal, not the load-bearing refrain or acrostic, which rest on the open primary.
